title: Chapter 4 Drill: Epilepsy and Episodic Disorders

items.stem: A 74-year-old man faints while shaving and turning his head. An electrocardiogram is normal. Carotid sinus massage under monitoring produces a 4 second pause. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Syncope triggered by head turning or neck pressure, with a pause of three seconds or more on carotid sinus massage, defines carotid sinus hypersensitivity, an older adult condition that may need cardiac pacing. Vasovagal syncope follows emotional or orthostatic triggers, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome affects younger patients with persistent tachycardia, and a seizure would not be reproduced by neck pressure.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has been convulsing continuously for 6 minutes when paramedics arrive. According to current guidelines, which definition and action apply?
options: Status epilepticus, so give a benzodiazepine now
Not yet status epilepticus, so wait 20 minutes
items.explanation: Current guidelines treat a generalized convulsion lasting five minutes or more as status epilepticus because it is unlikely to stop by itself, so first-line benzodiazepine therapy should begin immediately. The older 30 minute definition is no longer used for treatment decisions. Waiting an additional 20 minutes or calling a prolonged seizure an isolated event delays therapy and raises the risk of neuronal injury and drug resistance.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with a right frontal meningioma has a witnessed convulsion and then cannot move his left arm well. The weakness resolves fully over three hours, and repeat imaging shows no new lesion. What best explains the weakness?
options: Hemorrhage into the meningioma with new mass effect
Postictal (Todd) paresis from transient neuronal depression
Transient ischemic attack of the right middle cerebral artery
Functional conversion weakness triggered by the seizure
items.explanation: Transient focal weakness after a seizure, contralateral to the focus and resolving within hours to a day, is Todd paresis, attributed to postictal neuronal depression. Tumor hemorrhage would leave a lesion on imaging and persistent deficit, and a transient ischemic attack would not follow a witnessed convulsion with a clear precipitant. Functional weakness is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not needed when a recognized postictal phenomenon fits.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman remains awake and answers questions while her right hand develops rhythmic clonic jerking that marches up the forearm. Moments later she loses consciousness and has a bilateral convulsion. What is the correct ILAE 2017 classification?
options: Focal impaired awareness motor onset to bilateral tonic-clonic
Generalized onset tonic-clonic seizure from the start
Focal aware motor onset to bilateral tonic-clonic
items.explanation: Awareness is preserved during the initial unilateral clonic phase, so the onset is focal aware with motor features, and spread to both hemispheres defines evolution to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Impaired awareness at onset would not fit because she answers questions. Generalized onset requires bilateral involvement from the start, and unknown onset is used only when the beginning was not observed, which is not the case here.

items.stem: A 12-year-old girl has repeated episodes of loss of consciousness with brief convulsive movements while swimming or startled by a loud noise. Her sister had an unexplained drowning. Which test is most useful?
options: Electrocardiogram with measurement of the QTc interval
items.explanation: Events triggered by swimming, startle, or exertion with a family history of sudden death suggest congenital long QT syndrome, in which ventricular arrhythmia causes convulsive syncope that is easily mistaken for epilepsy, so an electrocardiogram is the key test. Imaging, electromyography, and lumbar puncture do not detect a repolarization abnormality. Beta blockers are the usual treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man with drug-resistant focal epilepsy that is not resectable is offered deep brain stimulation. Which target has randomized evidence for this indication?
items.explanation: Stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus reduced seizure frequency in a randomized trial of adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and is approved for this use. The subthalamic nucleus and globus pallidus interna are targets for Parkinson disease and dystonia, and the ventral intermediate nucleus is used for tremor, not epilepsy. Benefit tends to grow over the first years of therapy.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has dozens of brief arm and face jerks daily, followed by memory loss and hyponatremia. Magnetic resonance imaging shows medial temporal hyperintensity. Which antibody is most likely?
items.explanation: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures, limbic encephalitis with amnesia, and hyponatremia are characteristic of anti-LGI1 encephalitis, which responds to immunotherapy and often fails to respond to standard antiseizure drugs. Anti-GAD65 more often causes stiff person syndrome or refractory temporal epilepsy, while anti-aquaporin-4 and anti-MOG antibodies are associated with optic neuritis and myelitis rather than faciobrachial seizures. Early recognition matters because immunotherapy can reverse the syndrome.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has fever, confusion, and a focal seizure. The electroencephalogram shows repetitive sharp discharges over the left temporal region about once every second. Which diagnosis do these findings most strongly support?
items.explanation: Lateralized periodic discharges over a temporal region in a febrile, confused patient with seizures strongly suggest herpes simplex encephalitis, which should prompt empiric acyclovir pending cerebrospinal fluid testing. Hepatic encephalopathy produces bilateral triphasic waves, absence status shows generalized 3 Hz spike and wave without fever, and hypoglycemic coma produces diffuse slowing rather than focal periodic complexes.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman describes episodes that begin with a rising epigastric sensation and a feeling of intense familiarity. She then stares, smacks her lips, and fumbles with her clothing for about 90 seconds, followed by confusion. Where is the seizure most likely arising?
options: Supplementary motor area of the frontal lobe
items.explanation: A rising epigastric sensation, deja vu, and oroalimentary automatisms followed by postictal confusion form the classic mesial temporal semiology. Occipital onset produces elementary visual phenomena, supplementary motor area seizures cause brief asymmetric tonic posturing with preserved awareness, and parietal onset produces somatosensory or spatial symptoms. None of these produces the combination of visceral aura and automatisms described here.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man in the intensive care unit is receiving a continuous anesthetic infusion for refractory status epilepticus. The treating team asks for the electroencephalographic target of therapy. Which pattern is typically sought?
items.explanation: Titration to burst suppression, or at least seizure suppression, is the usual goal when an anesthetic infusion is used for refractory status epilepticus, guided by continuous electroencephalographic monitoring. Generalized periodic discharges indicate ongoing cortical irritability and an inadequate effect, an alpha coma pattern signals severe brain injury, and a posterior alpha rhythm is the normal awake background and would not be seen under such depth of anesthesia.

items.stem: A 60 kg adult is brought in with generalized convulsions for 7 minutes and no intravenous access. Which first-line treatment is best supported by trial evidence?
options: Intravenous phenobarbital 5 mg per kg first
items.explanation: Intramuscular midazolam at 10 mg for patients above 40 kg was at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam when no access is available, and it acts quickly. Intramuscular phenytoin is erratically absorbed and causes tissue injury, oral medication cannot be given to a convulsing patient, and phenobarbital is a later option rather than first-line therapy.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman taking carbamazepine and a combined oral contraceptive reports breakthrough bleeding. Which mechanism explains the concern for contraceptive failure?
options: Carbamazepine raises sex hormone binding globulin only
Hepatic enzyme induction increases hormone clearance
items.explanation: Carbamazepine induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accelerates clearance of ethinyl estradiol and progestins and can cause contraceptive failure, so alternative contraception or a nonenzyme inducing drug should be considered. Intestinal absorption is not blocked, binding globulin changes are a minor effect, and estrogen does not inhibit carbamazepine metabolism in a way that explains reduced contraceptive efficacy.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman has new focal epilepsy after a stroke. She takes warfarin, has osteoporosis, and has mild cognitive impairment. Which drug choice is most appropriate?
items.explanation: Lamotrigine is well tolerated in older adults, has little enzyme induction and minimal interaction with warfarin, and carries low risk for bone loss and cognitive slowing. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital induce hepatic enzymes, which alters warfarin control and worsens bone density, and phenobarbital and phenytoin also impair cognition and balance, which raises the risk of falls and fractures.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with poor oral intake is brought in after a generalized convulsion, and his serum sodium is 112 mmol/L. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Provoked seizure, so correct sodium cautiously
Start lifelong antiseizure therapy and nothing else
Correct sodium to normal within six hours quickly
Diagnose epilepsy and withhold any sodium correction
items.explanation: Severe hyponatremia is an acute symptomatic cause of seizures, which should be managed by treating the metabolic derangement, with sodium raised slowly, no more than about 8 mmol/L per day in most patients, to avoid osmotic demyelination. Lifelong drug therapy is not needed for a provoked event, and rapid normalization risks pontine injury, nor should the metabolic cause be ignored.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has daily staring spells with 3 Hz generalized spike and wave and no convulsions. Which drug is the best initial choice?
items.explanation: Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for childhood absence epilepsy without generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and a large randomized trial found it equal in efficacy to valproate with fewer attentional side effects. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are sodium channel blockers that can aggravate absence seizures, and gabapentin is ineffective for generalized absence seizures. The drug is also well tolerated by most children.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has drug-resistant seizures after failing two appropriately chosen drugs. Video electroencephalography, imaging, and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography show concordant right anterior temporal findings. What is the best next step?
options: Trial of a third and fourth drug before referral
Ketogenic diet as the only next option
items.explanation: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy, and the chance of seizure freedom with further drugs is low, so referral to a comprehensive center for surgical evaluation is indicated, particularly with concordant temporal findings. Delaying for additional drug trials or years of observation exposes the patient to continued seizures and injury, and diet is a lesser option than resection.

items.stem: A 29-year-old left-handed man with left temporal epilepsy is planned for resection. The team needs to determine language dominance and memory risk. Which test is traditionally used?
items.explanation: The intracarotid amobarbital test anesthetizes one hemisphere in turn to assess language lateralization and memory function before temporal resection, and functional magnetic resonance imaging is a noninvasive alternative for language. Evoked potentials and nerve conduction studies assess sensory pathways or peripheral nerves and give no information about hemispheric language or memory function. Left-handed patients are more likely to have atypical language organization.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman 36 weeks pregnant has headache, blood pressure 170/110 mm Hg, proteinuria, and a generalized convulsion. Which is the best drug to prevent further seizures?
items.explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for treatment and prevention of eclamptic seizures, and it was superior to phenytoin and diazepam in randomized trials, along with blood pressure control and delivery planning. Phenytoin and diazepam were less effective at preventing recurrence, and oral carbamazepine cannot be loaded quickly and is not used for eclampsia.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man with epilepsy asks which factor most increases his risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. What is the best answer?
options: Well controlled absence seizures during childhood years
Long seizure-free years on a stable treatment
Frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures at night
A single provoked seizure with a clear metabolic cause
items.explanation: Frequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures, particularly nocturnal and unsupervised ones, are the strongest modifiable risk factor for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, so achieving seizure control and nighttime supervision lowers risk. Well controlled childhood absence seizures, long seizure-free periods, and a single provoked seizure are associated with little or no increase in this risk. Adherence to medication also reduces the risk meaningfully.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman taking topiramate for focal epilepsy reports word finding difficulty, paresthesias, and flank pain with hematuria. Which adverse effect most likely explains the flank pain?
options: Renal tubular necrosis from direct toxicity
items.explanation: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase, producing metabolic acidosis and alkaline urine with low citrate that predispose to calcium phosphate kidney stones, and it also causes paresthesias and cognitive slowing with word finding difficulty. It does not cause hypercalcemia, direct tubular necrosis, or immunosuppression, so flank pain with hematuria is best explained by stones. Hydration and dose reduction can lower the risk of stones.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man has clusters of abrupt nocturnal awakenings with violent bicycling leg movements, shouting, and arm thrashing. Each lasts 20 seconds with immediate recovery, and he recalls the events afterward. Which localization is most likely?
options: Occipital lobe near the calcarine cortex
items.explanation: Brief, stereotyped hypermotor events arising from sleep in clusters, with rapid recovery and preserved recall, are characteristic of frontal lobe seizures. Mesial temporal seizures are longer and feature an aura with automatisms and postictal confusion. Occipital seizures begin with visual symptoms and eye deviation, and parietal onset usually produces somatosensory or disorientation symptoms rather than violent hypermotor behavior during sleep.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man started on lamotrigine 100 mg daily develops a diffuse rash on day 12. He is also taking valproate. Which factor most likely contributed?
options: Valproate induced the hepatic metabolism of lamotrigine
Valproate raised lamotrigine levels with fast titration
Lamotrigine always causes rash by day 12
items.explanation: Valproate inhibits glucuronidation and roughly doubles lamotrigine exposure, so combining them with a rapid starting dose raises the risk of a serious rash, and slow titration with halved starting doses is required. Valproate does not induce lamotrigine metabolism, lamotrigine has no effect on valproate absorption, and rash does not occur in every patient at a fixed time.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has focal impaired awareness seizures, and the clinical team suspects hippocampal sclerosis. Which magnetic resonance imaging approach is most sensitive?
options: Thick axial T1 images after gadolinium without FLAIR sequences
Thin coronal FLAIR and T2 sequences perpendicular to the hippocampus
Diffusion tensor imaging of the corpus callosum fibers alone
Susceptibility weighted images of the posterior fossa structures
items.explanation: A dedicated epilepsy protocol uses high-field, thin-section coronal FLAIR and T2 images oriented perpendicular to the long axis of the hippocampus, which reveal atrophy, increased signal, and loss of internal architecture. Thick contrast-enhanced axial T1 images miss subtle sclerosis, and diffusion tensor imaging of callosal fibers or susceptibility imaging of the cerebellum has no role in detecting mesial temporal pathology.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has stereotyped spells of sudden nausea, ictal vomiting, and unresponsiveness lasting one minute. Speech afterward is fluent and normal. Which focus does ictal vomiting most reliably suggest?
items.explanation: Ictal vomiting is a lateralizing sign that points to the nondominant, usually right, temporal lobe, and fluent postictal speech agrees with a nondominant focus. Postictal aphasia or ictal speech arrest would suggest the dominant temporal lobe. Frontal opercular seizures cause facial and oral motor symptoms, and primary motor cortex seizures cause focal clonic activity rather than autonomic vomiting.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry will begin treatment for focal epilepsy. Before starting carbamazepine, which test is recommended because of the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
items.explanation: Carrying HLA-B*1502, which is frequent in people of Southeast Asian and Han Chinese descent, carries a strongly increased risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis with carbamazepine, and screening is recommended before starting it. HLA-B*5701 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity, HLA-DQB1 is not used for this purpose, and thiopurine methyltransferase activity guides azathioprine dosing. Screening should be done before the first dose is taken.

items.stem: A 5-year-old with refractory epilepsy is being considered for the ketogenic diet. Which underlying disorder is a contraindication?
items.explanation: The ketogenic diet is contraindicated in disorders of fatty acid oxidation, carnitine deficiency, and pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, where the body cannot use fat or ketones safely and the diet can cause decompensation. Glucose transporter deficiency is the main indication because ketones bypass the transport defect, and Dravet syndrome and epileptic spasms are recognized situations in which the diet can help.

items.stem: A 6-year-old previously healthy girl develops near continuous focal motor seizures of the right hand, progressive right hemiparesis, and decline in language over months. Imaging shows progressive left hemispheric atrophy. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis, cognitive decline, and unilateral atrophy in a child describe Rasmussen encephalitis, a chronic inflammatory disorder in which hemispherectomy is the definitive therapy. Sturge-Weber syndrome has a facial port-colored facial birthmark and leptomeningeal enhancement, hemimegalencephaly shows enlargement rather than atrophy, and Landau-Kleffner syndrome causes acquired aphasia without hemiparesis. Early surgery is considered once the diagnosis is secure.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy has brief hemifacial twitching and drooling on waking, and sometimes a nocturnal generalized convulsion. The electroencephalogram shows high-amplitude centrotemporal spikes that increase in sleep. What is the expected course?
items.explanation: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes typically begins in mid-childhood, with sleep-related facial seizures and centrotemporal spikes, and resolves by adolescence in nearly all patients. It does not usually lead to a developmental encephalopathy, drug resistance is uncommon, and it is a separate entity that does not convert to a generalized syndrome such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

items.stem: A randomized trial compared anterior temporal lobectomy with continued medical therapy in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy. Which finding is correct?
options: Medical therapy gave better seizure freedom
Both groups had similar outcomes at one year
Surgery was abandoned for excess mortality
Surgery gave far more freedom from disabling seizures
items.explanation: In a randomized trial, more than half of patients assigned to temporal lobectomy were free of disabling seizures at one year compared with about one in twelve on continued medication, with better quality of life. The findings contradict claims that medication does better or that results were equal, and the trial did not show excess surgical mortality that would make the operation unacceptable.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man with focal seizures from multiple foci is not a resection candidate. A vagus nerve stimulator is placed. Which adverse effect is most characteristic during stimulation?
items.explanation: Left vagus nerve stimulation commonly causes hoarseness or voice alteration, cough, and throat discomfort during the stimulation cycle, because the stimulus reaches the recurrent laryngeal fibers, and these effects can be reduced by adjusting settings. Visual field loss is the effect of vigabatrin, gingival hyperplasia is caused by phenytoin, and hyponatremia is a feature of carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine.

items.stem: A 2-year-old with intractable seizures, developmental delay, and microcephaly has a normal brain scan. The family asks which genetic test is most likely to yield a diagnosis. What should be ordered?
options: Karyotype alone without sequencing of any gene
Single gene SCN1A sequencing without a broader panel
Multigene epilepsy panel or exome sequencing
Mitochondrial DNA deletion testing without other studies
items.explanation: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies are genetically heterogeneous, and a multigene panel or exome sequencing offers the highest diagnostic yield and can change treatment. A karyotype detects only gross chromosomal changes, and testing one gene assumes a syndrome that the presentation does not specify. Mitochondrial deletion testing alone is too narrow for this broad presentation. Positive results can also guide drug choice and family counseling.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has monthly spells of altered awareness, and two outpatient electroencephalograms were normal. His examiner suspects some events may be nonepileptic. What is the best next step?
options: A repeat routine electroencephalogram scheduled next month
Empiric increase of his antiseizure drug dose without recording
Serum prolactin measurement used as the single test
items.explanation: Capturing typical events with simultaneous video and electroencephalography is the diagnostic standard when routine recordings are unrevealing and the diagnosis is uncertain. Another routine study has low yield, empirically increasing medication may expose a patient with nonepileptic events to harm without benefit, and serum prolactin is an unreliable adjunct that cannot by itself separate epileptic from psychogenic events.

items.stem: A 9-month-old girl has a prolonged hemiclonic seizure during a febrile illness, and similar events have occurred from mild warmth. Development is currently normal. Which gene is most likely to be affected?
items.explanation: Prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures in the first year, triggered even by mild warmth with initially normal development, are the typical presentation of Dravet syndrome, which results from loss of function in SCN1A. KCNQ2 variants cause neonatal onset seizures, CDKL5 variants cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with severe developmental impairment, and SLC2A1 variants cause glucose transporter deficiency with low cerebrospinal fluid glucose.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with generalized tonic-clonic seizures is considering pregnancy in the next year. Which antiseizure drug should generally be avoided because of the highest risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental effects?
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects, other major congenital malformations, and impaired cognitive development in exposed children, so it should be avoided in women of childbearing potential unless nothing else controls seizures. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest malformation rates among common drugs, and oxcarbazepine has a moderate risk profile that is less than valproate.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has had focal impaired awareness seizures since a prolonged febrile seizure at age 2. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a small, bright left hippocampus. Which statement about his epilepsy is most accurate?
options: Seizures usually remit without treatment by age 40
Surgery is contraindicated with hippocampal findings
Generalized spike and wave is expected interictally
Surgical outcome is favorable if medications fail
items.explanation: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis often follows an early prolonged febrile seizure and commonly becomes drug resistant, but anterior temporal lobectomy gives seizure freedom in a majority of well selected patients. Spontaneous remission is not typical, imaging showing sclerosis supports rather than prohibits surgery, and the interictal pattern is focal temporal sharp waves, not generalized spike and wave.

items.stem: A 7-month-old infant has clusters of flexor spasms on awakening and regression of social smiling. The electroencephalogram shows a chaotic, high-amplitude background with multifocal spikes. Which term describes this pattern?
items.explanation: Disorganized, high-voltage slowing with multifocal epileptiform discharges in an infant with epileptic spasms is hypsarrhythmia, the interictal hallmark of West syndrome. Three hertz spike and wave defines childhood absence, burst suppression alternates high-voltage bursts with flat periods and signals severe encephalopathy or deep anesthesia, and a photoparoxysmal response is a provoked generalized discharge during photic stimulation.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has frequent brief episodes of unprovoked laughing without mirth, along with early signs of puberty. He has also become behaviorally difficult. Which lesion is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Gelastic seizures with central precocious puberty are the signature of a hypothalamic hamartoma, a lesion that is intrinsically epileptogenic and often leads to cognitive and behavioral decline. Cortical tubers cause multiple seizure types and skin findings but not gelastic seizures with puberty. Mesial temporal sclerosis rarely appears at this age, and a posterior fossa tumor produces ataxia and hydrocephalus rather than laughing seizures.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man is brought in after repeatedly asking the same questions for 5 hours and cannot recall the morning. He recognizes his family, has no focal deficit, and the episode resolves within 12 hours. It began after he showered in cold water. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Isolated anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning, preserved personal identity, no other neurologic signs, and resolution within 24 hours, often after a physical or emotional trigger, is classic for transient global amnesia. Nonconvulsive status would show impaired awareness and electroencephalographic seizure activity, posterior infarction would have additional deficits, and Wernicke encephalopathy features ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Recurrence is uncommon and no specific treatment is needed.

items.stem: A 3-year-old child has early morning seizures, ataxia, and developmental delay. Cerebrospinal fluid glucose is low with a normal serum glucose, and lactate is low normal. Which treatment is most appropriate?
items.explanation: A low cerebrospinal fluid glucose with normal serum glucose indicates glucose transporter type 1 deficiency from SLC2A1 variants, where ketones supply an alternative brain fuel, and the ketogenic diet is first-line therapy. Sodium channel blockers do not address the metabolic defect, and adrenocorticotropic hormone and corticosteroids are used for infantile spasms and inflammatory syndromes, not this transport disorder.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman had her first seizure 4 months ago and has had none since starting treatment. She asks about driving. What is the best counseling?
options: Driving is permitted immediately in every region
Follow the local seizure-free period law
Drive only at night when traffic is light
items.explanation: Driving restrictions depend on local regulations, which usually require a seizure-free period set by the authority, commonly several months, and physicians should counsel on the requirement and document the discussion, while helping the patient find transportation. An immediate return to driving ignores the risk, lifelong prohibition is not generally required, and night driving is no safer for a person with seizures.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman is admitted after an intentional isoniazid overdose and has refractory seizures despite benzodiazepines. Which treatment is specific for this cause?
items.explanation: Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine, reducing gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis, so seizures are often resistant to benzodiazepines alone and respond to high-dose intravenous pyridoxine given with benzodiazepines. Thiamine treats Wernicke encephalopathy, calcium gluconate treats hypocalcemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity, and naloxone reverses opioid effects without effect on isoniazid seizures. Dosing is guided by the amount of isoniazid ingested.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman remains confused and mildly responsive 90 minutes after a convulsion stopped, with subtle eyelid twitching. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassurance that postictal states can last many hours
Lumbar puncture before any brain imaging is obtained
Observation overnight without any further testing at all
items.explanation: Persistent altered awareness well beyond the usual postictal period, especially with subtle motor signs such as eyelid twitching, should prompt urgent electroencephalography to detect nonconvulsive status epilepticus, which is treated like convulsive status. Simple reassurance misses a treatable emergency, and lumbar puncture before imaging or watching overnight without testing delays diagnosis. Treatment should not wait for a clear convulsion to recur.

items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has brief attacks of dystonic posturing of one arm lasting 15 seconds, always triggered by suddenly standing up from a chair. He remains aware, and attacks occur many times daily. Which treatment is most effective?
items.explanation: Brief dystonic or choreic attacks provoked by sudden movement define paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, often associated with PRRT2 variants and usually dramatically responsive to low-dose sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine. Levodopa is for dopa-responsive dystonia, acetazolamide is used in episodic ataxia type 2, and clonazepam is a less effective alternative. Doses far below those used for epilepsy are usually enough.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man taking phenytoin has a total level of 12 mg/L, and the dose is raised modestly. Two weeks later he has nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech with a level of 32 mg/L. What property explains the disproportionate rise?
items.explanation: Phenytoin metabolism by hepatic enzymes becomes saturated within the therapeutic range, so small dose increases can produce large, nonlinear rises in serum level and toxicity with nystagmus, ataxia, and dysarthria. Linear first order elimination would give proportional changes, autoinduction describes carbamazepine, which lowers its own levels over time, and phenytoin is not primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidney.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman has a 12-minute event of asynchronous thrashing with side to side head movements and pelvic thrusting. She resists passive eye opening and later recalls parts of the event. Which feature is most specific for a psychogenic nonepileptic seizure?
options: Injury sustained in the fall to the floor
Onset shortly after an emotional upset
items.explanation: Ictal eye closure maintained and resisted during an event is among the most specific bedside signs of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures, whereas eyes are typically open in epileptic convulsions. Incontinence and injury occur in both conditions and do not discriminate, and an emotional trigger is common in nonepileptic events but is also reported by patients with epilepsy, so it carries little diagnostic weight.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and new confusion has an electroencephalogram showing generalized, frontally predominant waves with a negative sharp component between two positive deflections at 2 per second. What is the most likely cause?
items.explanation: Triphasic waves are generalized, frontally predominant periodic complexes seen mainly in hepatic and other metabolic encephalopathies, often with an anteroposterior lag. Absence epilepsy shows 3 Hz spike and wave bursts with an abrupt onset, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease shows periodic sharp wave complexes at about one per second, and herpes encephalitis produces lateralized periodic discharges over the temporal region.

items.stem: A 28-year-old patient being recorded for a routine electroencephalogram shows frontal sharp transients synchronized with each eye blink and a slow downward deflection at the frontal poles. How should this be read?
options: Ocular artifact from the corneoretinal dipole
items.explanation: Frontal slow deflections that match eye blinks reflect the corneoretinal dipole moving with the eyelid, a classic ocular artifact. Rhythmic delta activity is a continuous rhythm and does not track blinks, frontal epileptiform discharges are independent of blinks and show a field that extends beyond the frontal pole, and triphasic waves are periodic generalized complexes seen in metabolic encephalopathy.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man with refractory Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is considering felbamate. Which serious adverse effect requires monitoring and informed consent?
items.explanation: Felbamate is reserved for refractory epilepsy because of the risk of aplastic anemia and hepatic failure, which requires blood count and liver monitoring and documented informed consent. Visual field constriction is the hallmark of vigabatrin, hyponatremia is linked to carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, and gingival hyperplasia is a well known chronic effect of phenytoin. This risk limits the drug to refractory cases only.

items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has episodes of vertigo, slurred speech, and clumsiness lasting hours, with interictal downbeat nystagmus. Stress and exertion trigger events. A CACNA1A variant is found. Which treatment is first-line?
items.explanation: Episodic ataxia type 2 results from CACNA1A calcium channel variants, causing hours-long attacks with interictal nystagmus, and acetazolamide reduces attack frequency and severity. Carbamazepine is useful in episodic ataxia type 1 and paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, sumatriptan treats migraine attacks, and levodopa does not alter this channelopathy. Genetic confirmation supports the diagnosis but does not change this therapy.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy sits up in bed about one hour after falling asleep, walks and mumbles with open eyes, and cannot be roused easily. He remembers nothing in the morning. Events occur about once a week and last 10 minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Complex behavior from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, lasting several minutes with difficult arousal and amnesia, is typical of NREM parasomnia in school-age children. Frontal lobe seizures are brief and stereotyped, occurring in clusters, REM behavior disorder occurs later in the night in older adults, and panic attacks cause full awakening with recalled fear.

items.stem: A 14-year-old girl has progressive action myoclonus, generalized seizures, and worsening ataxia, with a normal early development. Genetic testing shows a dodecamer repeat expansion in the CSTB gene. What is the diagnosis?
items.explanation: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with action myoclonus, ataxia, and a CSTB repeat expansion defines Unverricht-Lundborg disease, the Baltic myoclonus form, which has a relatively slow course. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is nonprogressive and lacks ataxia, Lafora disease causes visual hallucinations and rapid dementia with polyglucosan bodies, and Dravet syndrome presents in infancy with prolonged febrile seizures. Confirming the repeat expansion avoids unnecessary further testing.

items.stem: A 32-year-old man has had no seizures for three years on one drug, with a normal electroencephalogram and magnetic resonance imaging. He asks about stopping treatment. What is the best counseling?
options: Slow taper is reasonable; recurrence is about one in three
Withdrawal is unsafe in every patient after any seizure-free period
Abrupt discontinuation is preferred once seizures have stopped
Recurrence risk after withdrawal is nil in this situation
items.explanation: After a seizure-free interval of two years or more, a gradual taper over months is reasonable for suitable patients, accepting a recurrence risk of roughly one third, higher with abnormal imaging, an abnormal electroencephalogram, or a juvenile myoclonic syndrome. Abrupt discontinuation risks withdrawal seizures and status epilepticus, and the recurrence risk is never zero, nor is withdrawal prohibited for everyone.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has sudden episodes of vertigo in which he becomes pale, clings to his mother, and wants to lie down for a couple of minutes. He has no headache and a normal examination between spells. His mother has migraine. What is the likely diagnosis?
items.explanation: Brief attacks of vertigo with pallor, fear, and normal interictal examination in a young child with a family history of migraine are characteristic of benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, a migraine precursor. Meniere disease affects older patients and involves hearing loss and tinnitus, a posterior fossa tumor would cause progressive signs, and epileptic seizures would involve altered awareness.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman is diagnosed with psychogenic nonepileptic seizures after video electroencephalography captured typical events. What is the most effective initial management?
options: Escalating doses of antiseizure drugs until events stop
Benzodiazepine rescue given for every single event
Clear explanation and referral for psychotherapy
Discharge without any discussion of the finding itself
items.explanation: Effective management begins with a clear, nonjudgmental explanation that the events are real but not epileptic, followed by psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy and treatment of coexisting psychiatric conditions. Escalating antiseizure drugs and repeated benzodiazepines cause harm without benefit, and discharge without discussion leaves the patient with no pathway to treatment. Outcomes improve when the diagnosis is made early.

items.stem: A 17-year-old with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is started on carbamazepine by another clinician, and her morning myoclonic jerks and absences become more frequent. What is the best explanation?
options: Carbamazepine lowers serum drug binding of other agents
Sodium channel blockers can aggravate generalized seizures
An inadequate loading dose was given for her weight
Carbamazepine induces sleep deprivation in adolescents
items.explanation: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, and some other sodium channel blockers can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized genetic epilepsies, so they should be avoided in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Treatment should be switched to a broad spectrum agent such as levetiracetam or valproate. Serum protein binding, loading doses, and sleep effects do not account for the paradoxical increase.

items.stem: A 19-year-old stands through a long, warm, crowded service, feels lightheaded with tunnel vision and nausea, and falls. Bystanders see a few jerks lasting seconds, and he is oriented within a minute. Which additional history item would most strongly favor a generalized convulsive seizure over convulsive syncope?
options: Onset while standing in a warm room
Lateral tongue bite and long postictal confusion
Brief myoclonic jerks lasting under 15 seconds
items.explanation: Lateral tongue biting and postictal confusion lasting many minutes favor a true generalized convulsion. Premonitory lightheadedness, pallor, onset when upright in heat, and brief myoclonic jerks lasting seconds are all typical of convulsive syncope, which results from transient cerebral hypoperfusion and recovers quickly. These features are therefore expected in either condition's mimic and do not shift probability toward epilepsy.

items.stem: A 20 kg child is having a prolonged seizure and intravenous access is present. Which first-line lorazepam dose is appropriate?
options: 0.1 mg per kg, maximum 4 mg per dose
items.explanation: Intravenous lorazepam is given at 0.1 mg per kg to a maximum of 4 mg per dose, and it may be repeated once if seizures continue after about 5 minutes, always with attention to respiratory depression. A dose ten times higher would risk profound respiratory arrest, a dose ten times lower would be ineffective, and a dose of 5 mg per kg is far above any appropriate range.

items.stem: A 10-month-old infant with refractory epileptic spasms is treated with vigabatrin. Which long-term monitoring is required?
options: Periodic visual field and retinal assessment
items.explanation: Vigabatrin causes irreversible bilateral concentric visual field constriction, so periodic ophthalmologic assessment is required, including in infants through electroretinography when formal fields are impractical. Neutrophil counts are monitored with drugs such as carbamazepine and felbamate in some settings, audiometry is not part of therapy, and sodium monitoring is relevant for carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine rather than vigabatrin.

items.stem: A 17-year-old basketball player collapses during a game without warning and recovers within a minute. His father died suddenly at 40. Examination reveals a systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva. What is the best next step?
options: Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram before play resumes
Electroencephalogram and an antiseizure drug started at once
Head computed tomography only, then clearance to resume play
Tilt table testing as the first and only test ordered now
items.explanation: Exertional syncope without prodrome, with a family history of sudden death and a murmur that increases with Valsalva, suggests hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and a risk of arrhythmic death, so electrocardiography and echocardiography are required and play must be restricted. Treating it as epilepsy would miss the cardiac cause, and imaging the head or tilt testing is not the appropriate first test.

items.stem: A 6-year-old boy with developmental delay has frequent tonic seizures in sleep, atypical absences, and drop attacks. The electroencephalogram shows slow spike and wave at about 2 Hz. Which syndrome does he have?
items.explanation: The triad of multiple seizure types including tonic seizures, cognitive impairment, and slow spike and wave under 2.5 Hz defines Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Dravet syndrome starts in infancy with prolonged febrile seizures, childhood absence epilepsy lacks tonic seizures and developmental impairment with faster 3 Hz discharges, and Doose syndrome begins with myoclonic astatic seizures in a previously normal child.

items.stem: A 15-year-old boy has early morning myoclonic jerks that cause him to drop his breakfast, and one generalized convulsion after a night of poor sleep. His examination and magnetic resonance imaging are normal. Which syndrome is most likely?
items.explanation: Myoclonic jerks soon after waking, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after sleep deprivation, and a normal brain on imaging in an adolescent define juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Childhood absence begins earlier and lacks myoclonus, centrotemporal epilepsy produces focal facial seizures in sleep and resolves by adolescence, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome features multiple seizure types with cognitive impairment and slow spike and wave.

items.stem: A 5-month-old boy with developmental regression has clusters of epileptic spasms and hypsarrhythmia, and no structural lesion. Which is the preferred first-line treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone or intramuscular adrenocorticotropic hormone
Carbamazepine at a standard maintenance dose in infancy
Phenytoin loading followed by maintenance dosing
Observation until the spasms stop on their own
items.explanation: Hormonal therapy with adrenocorticotropic hormone or high dose prednisolone, or vigabatrin in selected causes, is the preferred first-line treatment for infantile spasms because rapid control improves developmental outcome. Carbamazepine and phenytoin are ineffective for epileptic spasms and may worsen them, and waiting risks permanent developmental harm because spasms rarely stop on their own. Treatment should start promptly after the diagnosis.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man with focal epilepsy has MRI-negative drug-resistant seizures. Scalp electroencephalography suggests a right temporal origin, and the team needs more precise localization before surgery. Which is the next step?
items.explanation: When noninvasive tests do not give a clear and concordant localization, invasive monitoring with stereotactic depth electrodes or subdural grids defines the seizure onset zone and maps eloquent cortex before resection. Repeating the scalp study adds little, and lumbar puncture and electromyography do not localize epileptogenic cortex. The recordings guide the surgical plan and the extent of resection.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy plans pregnancy and takes lamotrigine. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Stop all antiseizure drugs before conception
Daily folic acid and monitoring of lamotrigine levels
items.explanation: Women with epilepsy who may become pregnant should take daily folic acid, and lamotrigine levels fall markedly in pregnancy because of increased clearance, so serum monitoring with dose adjustment helps maintain seizure control. Stopping all drugs risks convulsions that endanger mother and fetus, valproate is the most teratogenic option, and withholding prenatal vitamins is unfounded.

items.stem: An 18-month-old girl cries after being scolded, holds her breath, turns blue, becomes limp, and has a brief stiffening before recovering in under a minute. She has pallor and hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL. What should be done?
options: Reassure the family and treat the iron deficiency
items.explanation: Cyanotic breath-holding spells after a provoking event are benign, may include brief stiffening, and are associated with iron deficiency anemia, which should be corrected. Antiseizure drugs are not indicated and add risk, imaging is unnecessary with a typical history and normal examination, and an anesthetic infusion is used only for refractory status epilepticus. Families should be taught to place the child on her side.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman continues convulsing 20 minutes after adequate intravenous lorazepam. Which statement about second-line therapy is most accurate?
options: Fosphenytoin was clearly superior to levetiracetam in the trial
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate were similar
Valproate is contraindicated in all adult patients
Second-line drugs should wait until after intubation occurs
items.explanation: A large randomized trial of benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus found levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate to have similar rates of seizure cessation, so choice depends on comorbidity, such as avoiding valproate in women of childbearing potential. No agent was clearly superior, valproate is not universally contraindicated, and second-line therapy should not wait for intubation. Rapid administration of any of them is more important than the choice.

items.stem: A healthy term infant has brief tonic seizures beginning on day 3, with a normal examination between spells. Her mother had similar seizures in the first weeks of life that stopped spontaneously. Which gene is most likely involved?
items.explanation: Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy is typically caused by variants in KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 potassium channel genes, with seizures starting in the first week and usually remitting within months. SCN1A is linked to Dravet syndrome, TSC1 to tuberous sclerosis, which has additional skin and brain findings, and ARX to X-linked infantile spasms and brain malformation with severe developmental impairment.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman reports brief episodes of colored flashing circles in her right visual field, followed by forced eye and head turning to the right. Which cortical region is the likely origin?
items.explanation: Elementary visual phenomena in one hemifield arise from the contralateral occipital cortex, so right field symptoms localize to the left occipital lobe. Right occipital onset would produce left field phenomena. Mesial temporal seizures give visceral and psychic auras instead of simple visual patterns, and a lone frontal eye field focus would explain eye deviation but not the preceding colored visual hallucinations.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man still has electrographic seizures after a benzodiazepine and two second-line drugs. He is intubated. What is the next appropriate step?
options: Repeat the same benzodiazepine dose every hour for 12 hours
Discharge him to home observation after brief monitoring
Start oral carbamazepine as the only added treatment
items.explanation: Seizures that persist after benzodiazepines and a second-line drug define refractory status epilepticus and call for a continuous intravenous anesthetic such as midazolam, propofol, or a barbiturate with continuous electroencephalographic monitoring, titrated to seizure suppression. Repeating a benzodiazepine alone is inadequate, oral drugs cannot be absorbed reliably, and home observation is unsafe in an intubated patient.

items.stem: A 14-month-old girl has a 2 minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure with a temperature of 39.5 C from a viral illness. She is alert 30 minutes later with a normal examination. What is the best management?
options: Lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging studies
Daily phenobarbital for two years of treatment
Reassurance and fever care without ongoing drugs
items.explanation: A brief generalized seizure with fever in a well-appearing child between 6 months and 5 years, with return to baseline, is a simple febrile seizure, a benign condition that does not require imaging, electroencephalography, or lumbar puncture. Daily antiseizure drugs are not advised because risks outweigh benefits, so parental reassurance and education are the correct approach.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has a first unprovoked generalized convulsion. His examination, electroencephalogram, and magnetic resonance imaging are normal. What is the approximate risk of a second seizure within two years?
items.explanation: After a first unprovoked seizure the recurrence risk over two years is roughly 30 to 40 percent, higher with an abnormal electroencephalogram, structural lesion, or nocturnal seizure, and highest in the first months. Almost no risk would not justify follow-up, ninety percent is far higher than observed data show, and a five percent risk understates the recurrence typical of unprovoked events.

items.stem: Video monitoring of a 33-year-old man shows right hand automatisms with left arm dystonic posturing during an impaired awareness seizure. Which side most likely harbors the seizure focus?
options: Left frontal lobe near the midline
items.explanation: Unilateral dystonic posturing lateralizes to the hemisphere contralateral to the posturing limb, while automatisms tend to occur ipsilateral to the focus. Left arm dystonia with right hand automatisms therefore points to the right temporal lobe. A left focus would reverse both signs. Midline frontal onset typically produces fencing or bilateral tonic posturing, and the consistent lateralized pattern argues against independent bilateral foci.

items.stem: An 8-year-old girl is referred for brief staring spells many times a day, and her routine electroencephalogram is normal. Which activation procedure is most likely to reveal the diagnostic abnormality?
options: Intermittent photic stimulation at low frequencies
Eye closure for ten seconds only
items.explanation: Hyperventilation provokes generalized 3 Hz spike and wave discharges in most children with untreated absence epilepsy, and it is the standard activation for this syndrome. Photic stimulation is useful for photosensitive generalized epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy but is not the most sensitive here. Eye closure alone and mental calculation are not recognized provocations for absence seizures.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man is told he has epilepsy after an electroencephalogram showed rhythmic sharply contoured positive spikes in the posterior temporal regions during drowsiness. He has never had a spell. What is the best interpretation?
options: Interictal discharges of temporal lobe epilepsy
Benign variant, 14 and 6 Hz positive spikes
items.explanation: Fourteen and six per second positive spikes in drowsiness are a well described benign variant, and overreading such patterns is a leading cause of epilepsy misdiagnosis. Temporal lobe interictal discharges are negative sharp waves or spikes, not positive spikes of this kind. Periodic lateralized discharges recur at regular intervals in an acute lesion, and sweat artifact appears as very slow baseline drift rather than rhythmic spikes.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has drug-resistant focal seizures arising from two independent foci, one in eloquent language cortex. Which device offers closed loop treatment based on recorded activity?
items.explanation: Responsive neurostimulation records cortical activity through leads placed at the seizure foci and delivers stimulation when it detects epileptiform patterns, which suits patients with one or two foci or eloquent cortex that cannot be resected. Vagus nerve stimulation is open loop, spinal cord stimulation is used for pain, and transcranial magnetic stimulation is not an approved treatment for epilepsy.
